title: Snuff bottle with boys at play
date: Qing dynasty (1644–1911), Daoguang mark and period (1821–50)
medium: Porcelain painted with underglaze cobalt blue and overglaze enamels (Jingdezhen ware) with coral and metal stopper

altText: A small porcelain bottle painted with colorful scenes of boys playing, with blue and enamel colors on white porcelain. A small coral-colored stopper sits in the neck of the bottle.

context: This small porcelain bottle was made at Jingdezhen in China during the Daoguang period (1821-50) of the Qing dynasty. Snuff bottles held powdered tobacco, which people sniffed, and were prized as small works of art that could be carried and handled. The record tags the decoration Boys and Playing.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny bottle with a painted picture of boys playing. It is as small as something you could hold in your hand. Look for the boys. What game could they be playing?
descriptions.g12: People in China used bottles like this one to carry a kind of powder. It is small enough to hold in your hand. Painters decorated it with boys at play, using blue and bright colors on white porcelain. What are the boys doing? Look for what they hold or where they stand.
descriptions.g35: This tiny bottle is a snuff bottle from Qing dynasty China. Snuff is a powder made from tobacco, and people carried it in small bottles that were also meant to be admired. The painter decorated it with boys at play in blue and colored enamels. Look at the boys' actions and the space around them. What do you think makes this a good scene for a small bottle?
descriptions.g68: Made in the Jingdezhen kilns during the Daoguang period, this porcelain snuff bottle combines underglaze blue with overglaze enamels, so painters could mix cool blue with bright colors. Scenes of boys playing were a popular theme and are often linked with wishes for many healthy children and a happy family, though readings vary. The painter must fit a story onto a tiny curved surface. How do the scale and shape of the bottle change the way you look at the scene?
descriptions.g910: This Daoguang-period snuff bottle shows how a small, portable object could still carry a complete scene. The painting uses underglaze cobalt blue together with overglaze enamels, creating contrast between cool blue and warmer colors. Children at play were a common decorative theme in Qing China and could suggest hopes for family prosperity, though the exact message depends on details we should check in the image. Consider how the painter composes a scene for a surface that curves away and is held in the hand.
descriptions.g1112: A Jingdezhen porcelain snuff bottle of the Daoguang period, this object reflects the Qing taste for small, intricately decorated personal objects. Its combination of underglaze blue and overglaze enamels shows technical range, while the subject of boys at play connects to widely understood auspicious imagery of children and family continuity. Yet one must distinguish between the image's possible symbolic function and its visual charm. How do portability, tactile experience, and miniature scale shape the way a narrative scene is painted and received?

teacherNote.context: A Qing dynasty (Daoguang period, 1821-50) porcelain snuff bottle from Jingdezhen. The specific game or activity shown should be confirmed from the image before class discussion.
directions: Have students design a scene for a miniature curved surface, such as a paper cylinder, and note challenges.
Compare children's play scenes across cultures in the archive and discuss which games appear in more than one.
Discuss why people create small, beautiful objects to carry, and what small treasures students carry.
